findings.issue: catalog() caches a rejected promise with ??= and never clears it, so a single transient API failure permanently breaks home, types and all detail pages for the life of the SSR process.
findings.suggestion: Reset catalogPromise when load() rejects (retry on next call), or wrap load() with a retry/backoff so the catalog self-heals.

findings.issue: Only the first request of each resolver is wrapped in try/catch, and the catch-all turns every error (including 5xx/timeouts) into 'Not found'; failures in follow-up fetches reject the resolver, which the server surfaces as Express's default 404 and the client as a silently cancelled navigation.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish 404 from other failures, add withNavigationErrorHandler (per the data-resolvers guidance) or RedirectCommand fallbacks, and render an app-level error page for non-404 failures.

findings.issue: Module-level response cache is hidden global state shared across all SSR requests, with no TTL or size bound, so 'live' API data is frozen for the process lifetime and memory grows with the API surface.
findings.suggestion: Move the cache into the service, bound it (LRU or entry limit) and add a TTL, or rely on HttpClient's transfer cache plus per-request scoping.

findings.issue: The 200 ms search debounce timer is never cancelled on destroy; typing then immediately clicking a Pokémon card lets the timer fire router.navigate('/') and hijack the navigation.
findings.suggestion: Register a cleanup with DestroyRef (or takeUntilDestroyed) that clears searchTimer.

findings.issue: value="{{ q() }}" is a controlled binding: once the debounced navigation lands it resets the input, clobbering characters typed in the meantime (and trimming the user's trailing whitespace).
findings.suggestion: Bind only once from the URL (e.g. plain readonly attribute or compare against the input's current value) instead of re-binding on every change.

findings.issue: allowedHosts: ['*'] disables the SSR host check; official guidance says keep an explicit production list and never use a wildcard.
findings.suggestion: Read an explicit host list from an env var (with localhost for dev) and keep the DNS-rebinding protection on.

findings.issue: The Title-service + effect title block is copy-pasted in four page components (also move.page.ts:86, ability.page.ts:47, type.page.ts:110) and only takes effect after hydration, unlike the two routes with static route titles.
findings.suggestion: Use the router's route title (static for /types, a small title resolver for detail routes) or a custom TitleStrategy, so titles are set in one place and before SSR serialization.

findings.issue: API-shape interfaces are duplicated (TypeResource here vs. page-data.ts:71 with different fields; MoveResource only in page-data.ts), inviting drift as the API evolves.
findings.suggestion: Extract the PokeAPI response interfaces into one shared types file (e.g. pokeapi.types.ts) consumed by both.

findings.issue: One 400-line module holds resolvers and view models for all five pages; fine now, but it will become the file every feature change touches.
findings.suggestion: Split per route (pokemon.resolver.ts, move.resolver.ts, …) once a second contributor works here; page-data.ts already has section dividers to cut along.

findings.issue: ng test script, Vitest/jsdom dev-dependencies and a spec tsconfig are all configured, but the app ships zero unit tests.
findings.suggestion: Add Vitest specs for the pure logic (util.ts helpers, pokemonRefsToCards, catalog filtering/sorting, move-table compareValues) — cheap to test and where regressions will land.

summary: This is a tidy, genuinely current-Angular codebase — resolvers feeding component inputs, signals throughout, modern SSR with a real 404 status and event replay — that I'd be happy to own. The merge-blocking work is all in the failure paths: a permanently cached rejected catalog promise, unhandled mid-resolver errors with no navigation error handler, and a couple of small client-side races in the search. One focused round of changes plus a handful of shared tests and this is an easy approve.
